Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gitea remember-me token hash mismatch — CVE-2026-56750 stolen-token indicator
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Concurrent Gitea account access from divergent IPs — persistent stolen remember-me session · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Gitea remember-me token hash mismatch — CVE-2026-56750 stolen-token indicator AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Gitea application/auth logs for the ErrAuthTokenInvalidHash condition raised when a remember-me (gitea_incredible) cookie is presented with a valid ID but a rotated/stale Hash. Under CVE-2026-56750 this event is the highest-fidelity signal that a token was stolen and replayed: the legitimate user's original token now mismatches because an attacker already rotated it, yet the attacker's DB session survives. Rationale: Anchors on the exact error symbol ErrAuthTokenInvalidHash named in the advisory and the /user/login autoSignIn path; per CVE-2026-56750 this specific hash-mismatch on a same-ID token is the compromise indicator the Paragonie spec says must trigger full revocation but Gitea silently swallows. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rgv6-xp99-6mgj • https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/blob/689ace1ce28fd74244b8aa335d9928cdbf6b22f9/services/auth/auth_token.go#L33-L64
ATT&CKT1539 T1550.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User restored a browser profile/cookie backup and replayed an already-rotated remember-me cookie
  • Same account signed in on two devices where one held a stale gitea_incredible cookie
  • Reverse proxy / load balancer caching or rewriting the Set-Cookie causing a stale hash on retry
  • Browser prefetch or duplicated tab replaying the pre-rotation cookie once
  • Corrupted local cookie storage producing a benign hash mismatch
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientIP in ("<known corporate egress IPs are excluded via a watchlist>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the GiteaUser and every src_ip that triggered the mismatch; confirm whether one IP/geo/user-agent is unexpected for that account. 2) Contain: on Gitea host, delete ALL auth_token DB rows for that user (the fix Gitea omitted), force a password reset, revoke PATs/SSH keys, and upgrade Gitea to >=1.27.0. 3) Hunt: search for the attacker src_ip authenticating to other accounts, repository clones/pulls, new deploy keys, or webhook edits made from the surviving session after the mismatch timestamp.
let Lookback = 7d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ProcessName has "gitea" or SyslogMessage has "gitea"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("ErrAuthTokenInvalidHash", "invalid hash", "auth_token")
| where SyslogMessage has "invalid" or SyslogMessage has "mismatch"
| extend GiteaUser = extract(@"user(?:name)?=([^\s,]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend ClientIP = extract(@"(?:client_ip|remote_addr|clientIP)=([0-9a-fA-F\.:]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, GiteaUser, ClientIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gitea Remember-Me Token Hash Mismatch (CVE-2026-56750)
id: 6f3c1e2a-9b4d-4c7e-8a1f-2d5e6f7a8b9c
status: experimental
description: Detects Gitea logging a remember-me (gitea_incredible) auth token hash mismatch, indicating a stolen/compromised token per CVE-2026-56750.
references:
    - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rgv6-xp99-6mgj
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/21
tags:
    - attack.credential_access
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1550.004
logsource:
    product: gitea
    service: auth
detection:
    selection:
        message|contains:
            - 'ErrAuthTokenInvalidHash'
            - 'invalid hash'
    condition: selection
level: high
source:linux.syslog (ErrAuthTokenInvalidHash OR "invalid hash") gitea
APPLICATION
`gitea` message="*ErrAuthTokenInvalidHash*" 
| rex field=message "user(?:name)?=(?<gitea_user>[^\s,]+)" 
| rex field=message "(?:client_ip|remote_addr)=(?<src_ip>[^\s,]+)" 
| stats count AS mismatch_events, dc(src_ip) AS distinct_ips, values(src_ip) AS src_ips, min(_time) AS firstTime, max(_time) AS lastTime BY gitea_user 
| where mismatch_events >= 1 
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) 
| sort - lastTime
Concurrent Gitea account access from divergent IPs — persistent stolen remember-me session AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the same Gitea username authenticated/active from two or more distinct source IPs inside a short window, the observable side-effect of CVE-2026-56750: because the stolen token is never invalidated, attacker and victim sessions run concurrently. Pivots on parsed Gitea login events rather than the internal error, catching the persistence even when debug logging of ErrAuthTokenInvalidHash is off. Rationale: Uses the article's affected endpoint POST /user/login and the fact that the stolen token is never revoked, so victim+attacker sessions coexist; a per-user distinct-source-IP fan-out inside a 30m bin surfaces that concurrency without needing the internal ErrAuthTokenInvalidHash string. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rgv6-xp99-6mgj
ATT&CKT1078 T1550.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately logged in from office LAN and mobile/VPN simultaneously
  • CGNAT or mobile carrier presenting shifting egress IPs for one user
  • CI/CD or bot service account authenticating from multiple runners
  • User roaming between office Wi-Fi and home within the window
  • Corporate proxy pool rotating source IPs on each request
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientIP has_any ("10.", "172.16.", "192.168."))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the IPs set for the flagged GiteaUser — separate known corporate/VPN egress from unexpected geos/ASNs and correlate to the ErrAuthTokenInvalidHash hunt on the same account. 2) Contain: purge all auth_token rows for the user in the Gitea DB, force re-authentication and password reset, and patch to Gitea >=1.27.0. 3) Hunt: from the suspicious IP, enumerate repo clones, branch pushes, new SSH/deploy keys, PAT creation, and webhook/secret changes performed after the first divergent-IP timestamp.
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let WindowMinutes = 30m;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where ProcessName has "gitea" or SyslogMessage has "gitea"
| where SyslogMessage has "/user/login"
| extend GiteaUser = extract(@"user(?:name)?=([^\s,]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend ClientIP = extract(@"(?:client_ip|remote_addr|clientIP)=([0-9a-fA-F\.:]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(GiteaUser) and isnotempty(ClientIP)
| summarize DistinctIPs = dcount(ClientIP), IPs = make_set(ClientIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by GiteaUser, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where DistinctIPs >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog gitea "/user/login"
WEB
`gitea` uri_path="/user/login" (status=200 OR status=302) 
| rex field=message "user(?:name)?=(?<gitea_user>[^\s,]+)" 
| rex field=message "(?:client_ip|remote_addr)=(?<src_ip>[^\s,]+)" 
| bin _time span=30m 
| stats dc(src_ip) AS distinct_ips, values(src_ip) AS src_ips, min(_time) AS firstTime, max(_time) AS lastTime BY gitea_user, _time 
| where distinct_ips >= 2 
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) 
| sort - lastTime

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

SharePoint CVE-2026-50522 deserialization exploit: POST to /_trust/default.aspx with oversized WS-Federation body AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for unauthenticated POST requests to the SharePoint WS-Federation trusted-provider endpoint /_trust/default.aspx carrying an abnormally large request body, consistent with a forged SecurityContextToken cookie wrapping a .NET BinaryFormatter payload (the CVE-2026-50522 PoC delivery vector). Legitimate WS-Fed sign-ins hit the same endpoint, so this pivots on body size and per-source volume to surface the deserialization abuse. Rationale: Uses the article's exact abused endpoint (/_trust/default.aspx) and the WS-Federation POST vector for the forged SecurityContextToken; body-size threshold separates the oversized BinaryFormatter gadget from normal token sign-ins. Endpoint and vector confirmed by the original article and Janggggg PoC description. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-sharepoint-rce-cve-2026-50522.html • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-50522 • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SAML/WS-Fed federated sign-ins where the wresult token is genuinely large (rich claims, group SIDs)
  • ADFS/Entra token responses for users with many role claims exceeding 8KB
  • Load-test or synthetic-monitoring tools POSTing to the sign-in endpoint
  • Browser prefetch or retry storms inflating per-IP request counts
Suppression filter
| where UserAgents !has "HealthMailbox" and UserAgents !has "Load"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full IIS record for the top MaxBytes source IP; check whether the request carried valid federated auth material (per the article, PoC requests carry NONE) and whether scStatus 200/500 followed. 2) Contain: if unauthenticated and oversized, isolate the SharePoint server, block the source IP at the WAF, and confirm the July security update is applied. 3) Hunt: pivot to w3wp.exe child processes and .aspx writes on that host in the following 10 minutes (UC2/UC3), and rotate machine keys per watchTowr guidance.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/_trust/default.aspx"
| where csMethod == "POST"
| summarize RequestCount = count(), MaxBytes = max(csBytes), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), UserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by cIP, sSiteName, Computer
| where MaxBytes > 8192   // BinaryFormatter SecurityContextToken payloads dwarf legit WS-Fed SAML tokens
| order by MaxBytes desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime max(Web.bytes_in) as max_bytes values(Web.status) as statuses values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/_trust/default.aspx*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where max_bytes > 8192 | sort - max_bytes
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime max(Web.bytes_in) as max_bytes values(Web.status) as statuses values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/_trust/default.aspx*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where max_bytes > 8192 | sort - max_bytes
SharePoint w3wp.exe spawning command/script interpreter (CVE-2026-50522 RCE execution) AIExploitation High
Detects the IIS SharePoint worker process w3wp.exe spawning a shell or scripting host (cmd, powershell, mshta, wscript, certutil, etc.), the hallmark of successful CVE-2026-50522 deserialization RCE. SharePoint's w3wp rarely launches interpreters in normal operation, making this a high-fidelity post-exploitation signal regardless of the initial delivery vector. Rationale: Directly targets the RCE outcome of CVE-2026-50522 — the SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) executing an interpreter — a behaviour confirmed as an IOC across ToolShell/SharePoint deserialization writeups. High fidelity because SharePoint w3wp legitimately spawning shells is rare. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-sharepoint-rce-cve-2026-50522.html • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-50522/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint timer/health jobs or PSConfig/stsadm maintenance invoking cmd via the app pool
  • Sandboxed solution or custom web-part code legitimately shelling out
  • Monitoring agents (SCOM/Nagios) that execute checks under the SharePoint app-pool identity
  • Admin-triggered content deployment scripts running as the service account
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig","stsadm","Microsoft.SharePoint.Administration") and FileName =~ "cmd.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — recon (whoami/net), download (certutil/bitsadmin), or encoded PowerShell confirms exploitation; note the app-pool account. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, and preserve w3wp memory; block any C2 the child contacted. 3) Hunt: search the same host for .aspx webshell writes (UC3) and machineKey extraction commands (UC4), then rotate machine keys and app-pool/service-account credentials.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","hostname.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\net.exe","\\whoami.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: IIS SharePoint worker w3wp.exe spawning a shell or scripting host, indicative of CVE-2026-50522 deserialization RCE.

ASPX webshell dropped into SharePoint LAYOUTS/masterpage by w3wp (CVE-2026-50522 persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of .aspx files in SharePoint hive directories (TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS, _catalogs\masterpage, Web Server Extensions) by the IIS worker or a spawned interpreter, the persistence step following CVE-2026-50522 exploitation. Attackers plant webshells (e.g. ToolShell's spinstall0.aspx pattern) to keep access and exfiltrate the stolen machine keys. Rationale: Ties the article's post-exploit persistence goal (maintain access after patching) to the concrete artifact of an .aspx webshell written into SharePoint hive paths by w3wp — the same shape as ToolShell's spinstall0.aspx machine-key dropper. Constrained to SharePoint dirs + suspicious writer to keep FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-50522/
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SharePoint solution (WSP) deployment or cumulative update copying .aspx layout pages
  • Developer/admin manually staging a custom application page into LAYOUTS
  • Third-party SharePoint add-in installers writing masterpage assets
  • PSConfig/upgrade provisioning refreshing hive files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "psconfig" and FolderPath !has "\\CONFIG\\Upgrade\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written .aspx and check for machineKey/ValidationKey references, ViewState decoders, or command-exec stubs; capture SHA256 and compare to known ToolShell webshells. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and remove IIS caching of the page; block associated source IPs. 3) Hunt: enumerate all .aspx created org-wide in SharePoint dirs in the incident window, review IIS access to the dropped file's URL, and rotate machine keys immediately (patching alone leaves stolen keys valid).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName endswith ".aspx"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS\", @"\_catalogs\masterpage", @"\Web Server Extensions\", @"\wwwroot\wss\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".aspx"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS\", @"\_catalogs\masterpage", @"\Web Server Extensions\")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("w3wp.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint machine-key extraction via command line (CVE-2026-50522 credential theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for process command lines referencing SharePoint/ASP.NET machine-key material (MachineKey, ValidationKey, DecryptionKey, Get-SPMachineKey) executed by w3wp or spawned interpreters — the core objective of CVE-2026-50522, where attackers pull machine keys to forge SecurityContextTokens and persist post-patch. Stolen keys let an attacker mint valid auth tokens to impersonate any user. Rationale: Targets the article's headline objective — theft of SharePoint machine keys to forge valid SecurityContextTokens and survive patching — via the specific credential strings an attacker's PowerShell/webshell uses to read the keys. watchTowr and IONIX confirm single-request machine-key exfiltration. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-sharepoint-rce-cve-2026-50522.html • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-50522/ • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-50522
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1606.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint/IIS admin legitimately running Get-SPMachineKey or Set-SPMachineKey during a planned key rotation
  • DevOps automation reading web.config machineKey for a config-drift audit
  • Migration tooling exporting machineKey to sync a new farm member
  • Security team's own post-incident key-rotation activity
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName in~ ("sp_admin","svc_spfarm") and ProcessCommandLine has "Set-SPMachineKey")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the invoking account/host is an authorized SharePoint admin and whether the activity maps to a change ticket; check the parent process (w3wp/webshell parentage = malicious). 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the server and immediately rotate ASP.NET machine keys across the entire farm — stolen keys remain valid until rotated even after patching. 3) Hunt: review AAD/token issuance for anomalous SecurityContextToken/SAML usage impersonating users, and correlate with the w3wp spawn (UC2) and webshell drop (UC3) on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("MachineKey","ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","Get-SPMachineKey","MachineKeySection","GetApplicationConfig")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("MachineKey","ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","Get-SPMachineKey","MachineKeySection")
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

@vitest/browser Browser Mode API exposed to non-loopback network (inbound to node/vitest) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for a Node.js process running Vitest that accepts inbound connections from non-loopback/remote source IPs — the exact precondition (test.api.host set / dev server reachable off-box) under which the vulnerable provider commands can be reached by an untrusted client despite allowWrite:false. Article-specific because it pins on node.exe whose command line contains 'vitest' rather than generic dev-server exposure. Rationale: Anchors on node.exe with 'vitest' in the command line accepting inbound connections from a non-loopback IP — GHSA-p63j-vcc4-9vmv states the bypass 'matters most when the Browser Mode API is exposed to the network (test.api.host set / dev server reachable from another machine)'. Cross-checked the GitHub advisory text. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p63j-vcc4-9vmv
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally binds the Vitest UI/browser server to 0.0.0.0 for a teammate's device on the LAN
  • CI runner where the orchestrator connects to the test container's exposed port
  • Reverse proxy / VS Code Remote / dev-container forwarding that surfaces as a non-loopback inbound peer
  • Local mobile-device testing where a phone on the same subnet hits the Vitest dev server
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "169.254.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the listener is Vitest Browser Mode and check the running version (`npm ls @vitest/browser`) against the vulnerable ranges (>=4.0.0 <4.1.10, <3.2.7, >=5.0.0-beta.1 <5.0.0-beta.6); identify the remote src_ip and whether it is a known dev/CI host. 2) Contain: if unpatched and bound off-loopback, restrict binding to 127.0.0.1 or firewall the dev-server port, and bump @vitest/browser to a fixed release. 3) Hunt: pivot to file create/delete and sensitive-file read events by the same node PID (UC2/UC3) to see whether provider commands were actually abused.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "vitest"
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" or (RemoteIP !startswith "127." and RemoteIP != "::1" and RemoteIP != "::")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc

Vitest Browser Mode provider command writes/deletes files outside project (node.exe PNG/zip to sensitive paths) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the write/delete impact of the takeScreenshot / screenshotMatcher / stopChunkTrace / deleteTracing provider commands, which write PNGs or trace .zip archives to attacker-supplied absolute or ../-traversed paths and can delete arbitrary files — all from the Vitest node process, bypassing allowWrite. Flags the node/vitest process creating or deleting .png/.zip artifacts (or deleting anything) in OS/persistence/out-of-workspace locations no legitimate test artifact directory would use. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete impact model: provider write commands emit PNG images / Playwright trace .zip archives to attacker-chosen absolute or ../-traversed paths and deleteTracing removes arbitrary files — so a node/vitest process creating png/zip or deleting files in OS/persistence dirs is high-fidelity. Confirmed against the GHSA affected-commands table. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p63j-vcc4-9vmv
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A test suite legitimately configured to write screenshots/traces to a shared ProgramData or public artifacts directory
  • Global npm/tooling installed under ProgramData that node touches during a run
  • Cleanup routines that delete stale trace files under a system-wide temp/cache path
  • Custom reporter that archives results into a non-project directory by design
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\" and FolderPath has_any (@"\playwright", @"\vitest", @"\test-results"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the exact FolderPath/TargetFileName and the node command line; confirm whether the target dir is a sanctioned test-artifact location or a system/persistence path, and check @vitest/browser version against the vulnerable ranges. 2) Contain: if the write/delete lands in a system/startup/other-user path, isolate the host, preserve the file, and patch @vitest/browser; rotate any binaries that may have been overwritten. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (network exposure) and UC3 (sensitive file reads) from the same PID/session, and review who could reach the Browser Mode API when the operation occurred.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "vitest"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| where (FileName endswith ".png" or FileName endswith ".zip" or ActionType == "FileDeleted")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\", @"\System32\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup", @"\Users\Administrator\")
   or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)^[a-z]:\\[^\\]+\.(png|zip)$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe"

Vulnerable @sigstore/oci (<=0.7.0) npm package present on build/CI host (CVE-2026-59891) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the vulnerable @sigstore/oci package (all releases 0.1.0 through 0.7.0) landing under node_modules on developer, CI runner, or build hosts. This is the exposure surface for the substring-match credential confusion fixed in 0.7.1; finding where it is installed is step one of remediation. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable package scope path `node_modules/@sigstore/oci` named in GHSA-pf56-329r-95rw; presence of the package (patched only at 0.7.1) is the concrete detectable IOC. File-event telemetry fires at install/checkout time on CI runners and dev hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pf56-329r-95rw
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate installs of the patched 0.7.1+ package (file event has no version — treat every hit as a remediation candidate and verify version from package.json)
  • Transitive pull-through of @sigstore/oci via @actions/attest in a sanctioned CI pipeline that has already upgraded
  • Local npm cache / offline mirror re-hydration copying node_modules between hosts
  • Security scanner or SBOM tool unpacking the package into a scratch directory for analysis
  • Monorepo with multiple nested node_modules copies inflating hit count for one logical install
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !contains "\\.cache\\" and FolderPath !contains "/scanner/"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): On each hit, read `node_modules/@sigstore/oci/package.json` `version` field — anything <=0.7.0 is vulnerable; also check for @actions/attest and the actions/attest* workflow usage with `push-to-registry: true`. Step 2 (contain): Force-upgrade @sigstore/oci to >=0.7.1 (and the bundling @actions/attest / actions/attest* action versions) in the affected repo lockfiles; rotate any registry tokens present in that host's ~/.docker/config.json as a precaution. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC2 to check whether the affected host made outbound registry auth to any non-canonical registry host during a build window while the vulnerable version was installed.

Build tooling (node) authenticating to a first-seen / non-canonical OCI registry — @sigstore/oci credential leak in flight AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts for a node process on a build/CI host making outbound connections to a container-registry endpoint that is NOT one of the organisation's canonical registries and has never been seen before in the environment. This is the on-the-wire signature of CVE-2026-59891 sending ghcr.io/docker.io credentials to an attacker-controlled lookalike registry (e.g. cr.io matching a configured ghcr.io auth key) during the auth exchange. Rationale: Models the exploitation described in GHSA-pf56-329r-95rw: the substring-match flaw hands ghcr.io/docker.io credentials to a lookalike registry during the `/v2/` auth exchange. Anchors on node (the runtime for @actions/attest) egressing to a first-seen registry host that is not one of the article's canonical Docker Hub aliases (index.docker.io / registry-1.docker.io / docker.io) or ghcr.io. High FP by nature — scoped as a hunt over CI/build hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pf56-329r-95rw
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1048
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately new but sanctioned registry (a newly onboarded private registry or a partner's registry) contacted for the first time
  • npm/yarn resolving packages from a self-hosted mirror or Verdaccio instance that looks registry-shaped
  • Renovate/Dependabot or a container-scanning job pulling metadata from a public registry not on the allowlist
  • Cloud registry on a bespoke domain (self-hosted Harbor/Nexus/Artifactory) that should be added to the Canonical allowlist
  • Proxy/CDN fronting a canonical registry so the observed hostname differs from the allowlist entry
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".jfrog.io" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".harbor.internal" and RemoteUrl !has "nexus"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the destination host — is it a known org registry? WHOIS/registration age and whether the hostname is a substring-lookalike of a configured auth key (e.g. cr.io vs ghcr.io). Correlate with UC1 to confirm the host had @sigstore/oci <=0.7.1 installed and check the build's `subject-name` / `push-to-registry: true` inputs. Step 2 (contain): If the registry is unrecognised, block the domain/IP at egress proxy, quarantine the runner, and immediately revoke and rotate every credential in that host's ~/.docker/config.json (GHCR PAT, Docker Hub token, cloud registry token). Step 3 (hunt): Search all pipelines whose registry/image reference (subject-name) is influenced by untrusted input (PR titles, tags, external contributors) for the same non-canonical destination, and review the attacker registry IP across other build hosts.
let Canonical = dynamic(["ghcr.io","docker.io","index.docker.io","registry-1.docker.io","quay.io","gcr.io","registry.npmjs.org","mcr.microsoft.com"]);
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents

    | where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

| DomainName=/(registry|cr\.io|docker|ghcr|oci)/i

| sort(count, order=desc)

2026-07-21 6 use cases 1 technique 1 kill-chain phase detected

The Anubis ransomware gang has claimed responsibility for the cyberattack on Coca-Cola's Fairlife dairy subsidiary, threatening to publish allegedly stolen corporate data unless the company pays a ransom. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anubis ransomware execution via distinctive /KEY /PFAD /WIPEMODE command-line flags · [LLM] Anubis ransomware shadow-copy deletion via signature 'norealvolume' vssadmin string · [LLM] Anubis ransomware impact artifacts — .anubis extension and RESTORE FILES.html note · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Anubis ransomware execution via distinctive /KEY /PFAD /WIPEMODE command-line flags AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of the Anubis (Go-based) ransomware binary via its signature launch parameters — the German-named /PFAD= exclusion flag, the /KEY=<30+ char> encryption key, and the destructive /WIPEMODE wiper switch the article specifically calls out. This is family-specific, not a generic ransomware template. Rationale: Uses Anubis's documented, family-unique launch flags — /PFAD= (German 'path' exclusion), /WIPEMODE (the wiper the article emphasizes) and the /KEY=[A-Za-z0-9]{30,} regex — corroborated across Trend Micro, Picus and Barracuda write-ups, so any hit is high-fidelity to this specific binary. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/anubis-ransomware-targets-global-victims-with-wiper-functionality • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/anubis-ransomware-adds-wiper-to-destroy-files-beyond-recovery/ • https://blog.barracuda.com/2025/07/11/wipe--leak--extort--the-crazy-hybrid-playbook-of-anubis-ransomwa
ATT&CKT1486 T1485 T1134.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or reverse-engineer detonating an Anubis sample in an isolated lab host
  • Red-team/purple-team exercise replaying a captured Anubis binary against test assets
  • EDR sandbox / detonation appliance replaying the sample and logging its command line
  • A legitimate niche backup/crypto tool coincidentally using a /KEY= argument with a 30+ char value (rare)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("MALWARE-LAB01","DETONATION-VM") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\SandboxAgent\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full process tree for the hit — confirm the parent (unexpected parent such as a script host, PsExec, or a temp-dir Go binary ~5.4 MB) and whether /WIPEMODE is present (irreversible data destruction = P1). Check the executing account and host role (esp. hypervisor/Nutanix mgmt hosts). Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host immediately, kill the process, and preserve the binary + memory; if /WIPEMODE was seen, treat affected data as unrecoverable and escalate to IR lead. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the org for the same SHA256, for the .anubis extension and RESTORE FILES.html note (UC3), and for the norealvolume shadow-copy deletion (UC2) to scope lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/WIPEMODE" or ProcessCommandLine has "/PFAD=" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/KEY=[A-Za-z0-9]{30,}"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where CommandLine has "/WIPEMODE" or CommandLine has "/PFAD=" or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/KEY=[A-Za-z0-9]{30,}"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis ransomware shadow-copy deletion via signature 'norealvolume' vssadmin string AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Anubis's inhibit-recovery step, which deletes Volume Shadow Copies with the malformed hardcoded command 'vssadmin delete shadows /for=norealvolume /all /quiet'. The literal 'norealvolume' token is an Anubis artifact and is not produced by any legitimate admin or backup workflow, making this near-zero-FP. Rationale: The hardcoded 'norealvolume' volume token in Anubis's vssadmin invocation (documented by Picus/Trend Micro) is a unique family artifact with no legitimate equivalent, so it avoids duplicating the generic shadow-copy-deletion rule while giving near-zero false positives. Cross-checked against: • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/anubis-ransomware-targets-global-victims-with-wiper-functionality • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://areteir.com/resources/anubis-ransomware-group-global-threat
ATT&CKT1490 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating an Anubis sample in a lab (only realistic source of the exact string)
  • Red-team emulation deliberately reproducing Anubis's vssadmin command
  • Detonation sandbox replaying the binary
  • Effectively none from admin/backup tooling — no legitimate process passes /for=norealvolume
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the parent process of vssadmin.exe — a temp-dir Go binary, script host, or remote-session parent indicates ransomware, not admin activity; capture host and account. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the parent process chain, and snapshot/preserve remaining shadow copies on adjacent hosts before Anubis reaches them. Step 3 (hunt): Immediately pivot to UC1 (Anubis command-line flags) and UC3 (.anubis files / RESTORE FILES.html) across the fleet and check hypervisor/Nutanix management hosts, since shadow-copy deletion is the final pre-encryption step.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "delete shadows" and ProcessCommandLine has "norealvolume"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\vssadmin.exe"
| where CommandLine has "delete shadows" and CommandLine has "norealvolume"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anubis ransomware impact artifacts — .anubis extension and RESTORE FILES.html note AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Anubis's encryption impact on the file system: files renamed with the '.anubis' extension and the 'RESTORE FILES.html' ransom note dropped in affected directories. Both strings are Anubis-specific, so this is a direct, article-family hit rather than a generic mass-file-write heuristic. Rationale: The '.anubis' encrypted-file extension and 'RESTORE FILES.html' note filename are documented Anubis IOCs (Picus, Trend Micro); '.anubis' is not a legitimate extension so even a single write is malicious, and the aggregation surfaces the mass-encryption host and the initiating binary. Cross-checked against: • https://www.picussecurity.com/resource/blog/anubis-ransomware-targets-global-victims-with-wiper-functionality • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/f/anubis-a-closer-look-at-an-emerging-ransomware.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/anubis-ransomware-adds-wiper-to-destroy-files-beyond-recovery/
ATT&CKT1486 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Incident responders or threat-intel staff storing captured Anubis samples / ransom-note copies on a monitored host
  • Malware analyst detonating Anubis in a lab, generating .anubis files
  • Backup or forensic tooling copying already-encrypted .anubis artifacts during evidence collection
  • Security scanner quarantining and re-writing sample files that retain the .anubis extension
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Forensics\\" and DeviceName !in~ ("MALWARE-LAB01","DETONATION-VM")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the InitiatingProcess writing .anubis files (expect a temp-dir Go binary ~5.4 MB) and the rate/scope of file writes; confirm whether it is a live encryption run vs. stored evidence. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host, terminate the initiating process, disable the associated account, and protect file shares / hypervisor datastores the host can reach (Anubis encrypted Nutanix at Fairlife). Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with UC1 (launch flags) and UC2 (norealvolume vssadmin) on the same host and timeline, and sweep other hosts for the same initiating SHA256 and note filename to find additional encrypted systems.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".anubis" or FileName =~ "RESTORE FILES.html"
| summarize FileCount=count(), DistinctPaths=dcount(FolderPath), SampleFolder=take_any(FolderPath), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by FileCount desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".anubis" or TargetFileName endswith "RESTORE FILES.html"
| summarize FileCount=count(), DistinctPaths=dcount(TargetFilePath), SampleFolder=take_any(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| order by FileCount desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] wp2shell pre-auth exploit chain: /wp-json/batch/v1 route-confusion + author__not_in SQLi · [LLM] wp2shell LFI: wp-config credential theft via admin-ajax.php · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] wp2shell webshell dropped as PHP under /wp-content/cache/ by web server process · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] wp2shell webshell interaction: HTTP requests to executable PHP under /wp-content/cache/ · Network connections to article IPs / domains

wp2shell pre-auth exploit chain: /wp-json/batch/v1 route-confusion + author__not_in SQLi AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests hitting the WordPress REST batch endpoint (/wp-json/batch/v1) or carrying the CVE-2026-60137 SQLi parameter author__not_in. This is the entry point of the wp2shell chain (CVE-2026-63030 + CVE-2026-60137) and both markers are near-unique to exploitation attempts. Rationale: Both markers are corroborated as the two-CVE chain by Wiz, VulnCheck and The Hacker News: /wp-json/batch/v1 is the CVE-2026-63030 route-confusion endpoint and author__not_in is the CVE-2026-60137 WP_Query SQLi param — neither appears in normal traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-wp2shell-wordpress-core-flaw-lets.html • https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/wp2shell • https://github.com/0xWhoknows/wp2shell
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Wiz, Nessus, WPScan) probing /wp-json/batch/v1 — much of the observed traffic is benign security scanning per Wiz
  • Legitimate plugins/apps using the WP REST batch API for bulk operations (rare but exists)
  • Internal WordPress health-check or CI probes hitting the REST API
  • Bug-bounty researchers testing the disclosed PoC against your own assets
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["10.0.0.0/8"])) and DstHostname !has "staging"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the offending SrcIpAddr and check whether author__not_in payloads contain SQL syntax (UNION, SLEEP, quotes) and whether any batch request returned 200. Confirm the target's WordPress version is < 6.9.5 / 7.0.2 / 6.8.6. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, and if the host is unpatched force-update WordPress to the fixed version and take the site offline if exploitation succeeded. 3) Hunt: pivot to file-write telemetry for new .php under /wp-content/cache/ and /wp-content/plugins/, and check wp_users for admin accounts created after the first probe.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/wp-json/batch/v1" or Url has "author__not_in"
| summarize Requests=count(), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod,5), Statuses=make_set(HttpStatusCode,10), UserAgents=make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent,5), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| order by Requests desc

wp2shell webshell dropped as PHP under /wp-content/cache/ by web server process AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of .php files inside the WordPress /wp-content/cache/ directory by the PHP/web-server process — the exact persistence artifact SANS ISC documented for wp2shell (webshell created in /cache/ returning a fake 404). WordPress never serves executable PHP from its cache folder, making this high fidelity. Rationale: Grounded in the SANS ISC / Wiz finding that wp2shell writes its webshell into /wp-content/cache/ (fake-404 disguise); the PHP-interpreter-writes-PHP-into-cache combination is the high-fidelity behavior no caching plugin normally produces. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/18/wordpress-vulnerabilities-wp2shell-cve-2026-60137-cve-2026-60137/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WP Super Cache / W3 Total Cache legacy modes writing supercache .php meta files into wp-content/cache
  • WP Rocket or other page-cache plugins generating PHP config artifacts
  • A developer manually placing a debug .php in the cache dir
  • Object-cache drop-ins (redis/memcached) writing object-cache.php
  • Plugin auto-update processes rewriting cached PHP includes
Suppression filter
| where TargetFileName !startswith "wp-cache-" and TargetFilePath !has "/cache/wp-rocket/" and TargetFilePath !has "/cache/supercache/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the new .php file's contents (or hash it against threat intel) — webshells contain eval/base64_decode/assert/system and often a fake header('HTTP/1.1 404'). Confirm the writing process was php-fpm/apache. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, revoke web-server write access to the cache dir, and rotate the wp-config secret keys and DB credentials. 3) Hunt: search access logs for subsequent GET/POST to that exact cache path (webshell interaction), enumerate other .php dropped under wp-content, and audit wp_users for rogue admins.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "/wp-content/cache/"
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx","litespeed","lsphp")
| where FileName !in~ ("advanced-cache.php","object-cache.php","wp-cache-config.php") and FileName !startswith "wp-cache-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has "/wp-content/cache/" and TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx","litespeed","lsphp")
| where TargetFileName !in~ ("advanced-cache.php","object-cache.php","wp-cache-config.php")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA1, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

wp2shell webshell interaction: HTTP requests to executable PHP under /wp-content/cache/ AICommand & Control High
Hunts inbound requests to any .php file located under /wp-content/cache/ — post-exploitation interaction with the planted wp2shell backdoor. SANS ISC noted the shell returns a fake 404, so status code is unreliable; the path itself is the signal because WordPress never serves PHP from its cache directory. Rationale: Directly from the SANS ISC report (webshell created under /cache/ returning a fake 404); requesting an executable PHP from the cache directory is an unambiguous backdoor-interaction signal that is status-code independent. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/18/wordpress-vulnerabilities-wp2shell-cve-2026-60137-cve-2026-60137/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Caching plugins that legitimately serve a .php cache handler from wp-content/cache (rare legacy WP Super Cache setups)
  • Security scanners fuzzing common webshell paths under wp-content
  • Uptime/monitoring probes configured against a specific cache path
  • A developer's leftover debug PHP endpoint in the cache dir
Suppression filter
| where Url !has "/cache/wp-rocket/" and Url !has "/cache/supercache/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the requested cache-path .php with a matching file-write event (UC2). If the file exists on disk and analysts didn't create it, treat as confirmed webshell. Inspect POST bodies/params for command strings. 2) Contain: block the SrcIpAddr, delete the file, and rotate wp-config keys + DB creds. 3) Hunt: enumerate every SrcIpAddr that touched the path, review commands executed, and check for lateral movement, new admin users, and outbound connections from the web host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)/wp-content/cache/[^?\s]*\.php"
| summarize Hits=count(), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod,5), Statuses=make_set(HttpStatusCode,10), UserAgents=make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent,5), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| order by Hits desc

wp2shell LFI: wp-config credential theft via admin-ajax.php AIExploitation Medium
Hunts local file inclusion attempts against wp-config through admin-ajax.php — a wp2shell post-exploitation step Wiz observed to retrieve WordPress database credentials and authentication keys. Flags admin-ajax.php requests carrying wp-config references, path traversal, or php://filter wrappers. Rationale: Based on Wiz's observed activity: 'Local file inclusion attempts targeting wp-config through admin-ajax.php to retrieve database credentials and authentication keys' — admin-ajax.php combined with wp-config/traversal/php-filter markers is a precise LFI signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1083 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Plugins that legitimately pass file paths through admin-ajax.php actions (some backup/migration plugins)
  • Security scanners testing LFI payloads against admin-ajax.php
  • URL-encoded query values containing '../' as benign relative references
  • Analyst/pentest validation of the disclosed chain against owned assets
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the admin-ajax.php request actually references wp-config and check the response size/status — a large 200 suggests the file was disclosed. 2) Contain: block the source IP, and because wp-config keys/salts and DB creds may be exposed, immediately rotate all WordPress secret keys/salts and reset the database password. 3) Hunt: check whether the same IP later authenticated to wp-admin, created admin users, or dropped a webshell (UC2/UC3), and review DB access logs for the exposed credentials.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "admin-ajax.php"
| where Url has_any ("wp-config", "php://filter", "../", "..%2f", "..%252f")
| summarize Requests=count(), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod,5), Statuses=make_set(HttpStatusCode,10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| order by Requests desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-63030", "CVE-2026-60137")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-63030", "CVE-2026-60137")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or SHA1 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or MD5 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or SHA1 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f") or MD5 in~ ("2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2a1410d8e2a8337ac2171cedea8c0fdc47c647a0", "58eca847e9eae9e6b08cc211f1559817b71bc4cc", "ebea44890f434d5d67ede22009a3f4bb5cac33f8", "d9a220c8039f1c4d72cae7ccb8b3a33dec8815be", "e9756e2338f84746007235e4cab7a70d5b3ca47f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

AWS Kiro Flaw Let a Poisoned Web Page Rewrite Its Config and Run Code

The Hacker News
2026-07-21 14 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Hidden text on a web page was enough to make Kiro, AWS's agentic coding IDE, rewrite its own configuration file and run an attacker's code on a developer's machine, with no approval step able to stop it. Intezer, in research with Kodem Security, found that a request as ordinary as asking Kiro to summarize a page could end in remote code execution. AWS has patched the issue, and no CVE has been

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kiro process spawning shell / interpreter child (rogue MCP server start command) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Kiro (AWS agentic IDE) writing protected config files mcp.json / .vscode tasks.json · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Kiro-spawned interpreter beaconing to external host (rogue MCP server C2)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Kiro (AWS agentic IDE) writing protected config files mcp.json / .vscode tasks.json AIInstallation High
Hunts the core primitive of the Intezer/Kodem Kiro chain: the Kiro process itself writing ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json (which registers MCP-server start commands that auto-execute on reload) or .vscode/tasks.json / settings.json (CVE-2026-10591 auto-exec on folder open). A poisoned web page fetched by Kiro drives fsWrite to these files with no effective approval, turning a config edit into code execution. Rationale: Uses the exact article artifacts: the Kiro process (fsWrite) writing ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json and the .vscode/tasks.json|settings.json auto-exec files named in the Intezer, Rehberger (Embrace The Red) and Cymulate (CVE-2026-10591) findings. Constraining the writer to a Kiro process on these specific paths is the highest-fidelity form of the primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/aws-kiro-flaw-let-poisoned-web-page.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-10591 • https://embracethered.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1059 T1554 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately adding/editing an MCP server through the Kiro UI, which writes mcp.json normally
  • Format-on-save or workspace-trust changes rewriting .vscode/settings.json
  • Kiro adding a build/lint task to .vscode/tasks.json at user request
  • Extension or Kiro version update rewriting workspace config
  • Team member syncing a shared .vscode config committed to the repo
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bash","sh -c","python","curl","wget","nc ","osascript","base64") or FileName == "mcp.json"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the written mcp.json/tasks.json content (or nearest DeviceFileEvents delta) — inspect any newly added MCP server 'command'/'args' or task shell command for interpreters, curl/wget, or base64. Confirm whether the user was actively fetching/summarising an external URL at that time. 2) Contain: if the config references an unexpected binary or network callback, isolate the host, kill the spawned server process, and revert mcp.json/.vscode files; verify Kiro is on >=1.0.x (protected-paths fix). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for a Kiro-child interpreter and outbound beacon (UC2/UC3), and search other developer endpoints for the same injected server 'command' string.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has "/.kiro/settings" and FileName =~ "mcp.json")
     or (FolderPath has "/.vscode" and FileName in~ ("tasks.json","settings.json"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "kiro"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFilePath has "/.kiro/settings" and TargetFileName =~ "mcp.json")
     or (TargetFilePath has "/.vscode" and TargetFileName in~ ("tasks.json","settings.json"))
| where ActingProcessName has "kiro"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Kiro Agentic IDE Writing Protected Config Files (mcp.json / .vscode)
id: 3a1f2c5e-7b64-4d9a-9f21-8c0e5b1a4d77
description: Detects the Kiro AWS agentic coding IDE writing its MCP server config or VS Code task/settings files, the write-to-execute primitive abused by the Intezer/Kodem prompt-injection chain and CVE-2026-10591.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/aws-kiro-flaw-let-poisoned-web-page.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/21
tags:
  - attack.t1059

  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_kiro_mcp:
    ActingProcessName|contains: 'kiro'
    TargetFilePath|contains: '/.kiro/settings'
    TargetFileName: 'mcp.json'
  selection_vscode:
    ActingProcessName|contains: 'kiro'
    TargetFilePath|contains: '/.vscode'
    TargetFileName:
      - 'tasks.json'
      - 'settings.json'

level: high
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| (TargetFileName=/\/\.kiro\/settings\/mcp\.json$/i OR TargetFileName=/\/\.vscode\/(tasks|settings)\.json$/i)
| ContextImageFileName=/kiro/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="mcp.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.kiro/settings/*") OR (Filesystem.file_name="tasks.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.vscode/*") OR (Filesystem.file_name="settings.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.vscode/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="mcp.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.kiro/settings/*") OR (Filesystem.file_name="tasks.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.vscode/*") OR (Filesystem.file_name="settings.json" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.vscode/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
Kiro process spawning shell / interpreter child (rogue MCP server start command) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts execution of the injected MCP server: after Kiro reloads a poisoned mcp.json it launches the server's start command on the host with the developer's privileges. Surfaces Kiro as the parent of a shell or scripting interpreter (bash/sh/zsh/python/node/osascript/curl), which is how the attacker's arbitrary command runs. Rationale: Directly targets the article's execution step — Kiro launching the MCP server's start command as a host process with developer privileges. Kiro-as-parent of a raw shell/scripting interpreter (esp. osascript/curl/nc) is the anomaly; kept hunting-tier because Kiro legitimately spawns node/python for real MCP servers and its integrated terminal. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/aws-kiro-flaw-let-poisoned-web-page.html • https://www.intezer.com/ • https://embracethered.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.006 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MCP servers Kiro launches as node/python child processes
  • Developer using Kiro's integrated terminal to run bash/zsh/python
  • Kiro build/test tasks invoking shell commands
  • Language servers or linters spawned by the IDE
  • Git or package-manager hooks (curl/wget) triggered from the IDE terminal
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c ","base64","curl","wget","/tmp/","bash -i","osascript","IEX","Invoke-Expression") or FileName in~ ("nc","ncat","osascript")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read ProcessCommandLine of the child — legitimate MCP servers run known package paths; flag inline shell one-liners, base64, curl|bash, osascript, or reverse-shell tooling. Correlate the child's start time against a preceding mcp.json/tasks.json write (UC1) within seconds. 2) Contain: kill the child process tree, isolate the host if the command is clearly malicious, and revert Kiro config files. 3) Hunt: check the child process for outbound beaconing (UC3) and enumerate other dev hosts running the same command string or contacting the same destination.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "kiro"
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","python","python3","node","osascript","curl","wget","nc","ncat","pwsh","powershell.exe","cmd.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "kiro"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","/sh","zsh","python","node","osascript","curl","wget","/nc","ncat","pwsh","powershell")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Kiro Agentic IDE Spawning Shell or Interpreter Child

description: Detects the Kiro AWS agentic IDE spawning a shell or scripting interpreter, consistent with execution of a rogue MCP server start command written into mcp.json via prompt injection.
references:

date: 2026/07/21
tags:

detection:

level: medium
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/kiro/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(bash|sh|zsh|python3?|node|osascript|curl|wget|nc|ncat)$/i

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="kiro*" OR Processes.parent_process_name="Kiro*") AND (Processes.process_name IN ("bash","sh","zsh","python","python3","node","osascript","curl","wget","nc","ncat")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="kiro*" OR Processes.parent_process_name="Kiro*") AND (Processes.process_name IN ("bash","sh","zsh","python","python3","node","osascript","curl","wget","nc","ncat")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
Kiro-spawned interpreter beaconing to external host (rogue MCP server C2) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the C2 behaviour proven in Intezer's PoC: the rogue MCP server (a child of Kiro) phones home on a fixed short interval (every ~10 seconds in the demo) exfiltrating hostname, username and platform. Surfaces high-count, regular outbound connections from Kiro-child interpreter processes to an external destination. Rationale: Encodes the PoC's fixed ~10-second beacon of host/user/platform and ties the network activity to a Kiro-child interpreter (Defender via InitiatingProcessParentFileName; Sentinel via an ImProcessCreate->ImNetworkSession host+time join since ImNetworkSession carries no process attribution). Threshold-based, so Sigma is intentionally omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/aws-kiro-flaw-let-poisoned-web-page.html • https://www.intezer.com/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MCP servers (node/python) making frequent API calls to a remote endpoint
  • Kiro AI backend/telemetry connections polling a cloud service
  • Package managers (npm/pip) pulling dependencies via node/python
  • Developer scripts run from the IDE terminal polling an internal API
  • Language-model or linter processes streaming to a SaaS endpoint
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1") and Ports != dynamic([443])
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the RemoteIP/destination and the child process command line — whitelisted SaaS/MCP endpoints are benign; a raw IP, dynamic-DNS, or localhost-in-testing pattern plus fixed short intervals is suspicious. Confirm the connecting process descends from Kiro and correlate with a recent mcp.json write (UC1) and interpreter spawn (UC2). 2) Contain: block the destination, isolate the host, kill the beaconing process, and revert Kiro config. 3) Hunt: sweep other developer endpoints for the same destination IP/domain and identical mcp.json server 'command' string; assess whether credentials or source code left the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName has "kiro"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize ConnCount = count(), IntervalBuckets = dcount(bin(Timestamp, 10s)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 8)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| where ConnCount >= 30    // ~10s beacon sustained over several minutes
| order by ConnCount desc
let KiroChildren = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName has "kiro"
    | project DvcHostname, ChildStart = TimeGenerated, ChildProcess = ActingProcessName;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection))
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| join kind=inner KiroChildren on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ChildStart .. ChildStart + 1h)
| summarize ConnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ChildProcess, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount >= 30    // ~10s beacon sustained over several minutes
| order by ConnCount desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(node|python3?|bash|osascript|curl|wget|nc|ncat)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
| count >= 30
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="outbound" AND (All_Traffic.app IN ("node","python","python3","bash","osascript","curl","wget")) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where count >= 30 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="outbound" AND (All_Traffic.app IN ("node","python","python3","bash","osascript","curl","wget")) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where count >= 30 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - count

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10591")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10591")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
